tldr: CodePlan is a task-agnostic framework that frames repository-level coding as a planning problem, synthesizing multi-step chains of edits using LLMs guided by incremental dependency analysis, change may-impact analysis, and adaptive planning.
contributions: First formalization of automating repository-level coding tasks using LLMs, requiring analysis and propagation of code change effects across repositories
A task-agnostic framework (CodePlan) combining incremental dependency analysis, change may-impact analysis, and adaptive planning to synthesize multi-step edit plans for LLMs
Evaluation on two repository-level tasks: package migration (C#) and temporal code edits (Python), comparing against oracle-guided baselines
Results showing CodePlan gets 5/6 repositories to pass validity checks while baselines get 0/6
methods: CodePlan frames repository-level coding as automated planning, maintaining a plan graph (DAG) of edit obligations and a dependency graph tracking syntactic/semantic relations across the repository. It takes a repository, seed edit specifications, an oracle, and an LLM as inputs. For each pending edit node, it extracts a code fragment with surrounding class context, gathers spatial context (related code via static analysis) and temporal context (prior edits along plan graph paths), constructs a prompt, invokes the LLM, merges the result back, and updates the dependency graph. Change classification (modification, addition, deletion) drives a may-impact analysis that identifies affected dependent blocks, which are then added to the plan graph as new or extended edit obligations. This loop continues until the oracle validates the repository.
results: Evaluated on package migration (C#) and temporal code edits (Python) across multiple repositories requiring inter-dependent changes to 2-97 files. CodePlan achieved better match with ground truth compared to baselines. CodePlan got 5/6 repositories to pass validity checks (e.g., building without errors and making correct code edits), whereas baselines—which use oracles (build system for C#, static type checker for Python) to iteratively identify and fix errors without planning—could not get any of the repositories to pass.
limitations: Not all changes induce build errors even when they produce behavioral changes (e.g., changing a return value from True to False without changing the return type), which pure oracle-guided approaches miss
Build systems are agnostic to cause-effect relationships when code breaks, potentially leading to incorrect fixes (e.g., reverting seed changes)
The paper notes this is a complex problem and only evaluates on two tasks (package migration and temporal code edits); broader task coverage is not demonstrated
Some proprietary repositories were not released with the data and evaluation scripts
